The Adams $E_2$ page, from a minimal resolution of $\mathbb{F}_2$ over the Steenrod algebra.

  • One bidegree $(n, s)$ at a time, stem $n = t - s$.

The cost doubles every 16 stems

Stem 290 costs 72 times stem 200. The census through stem 300 performed 61 trillion Milnor products.

Single-node census. Fit over stems 150–299: +4.5% per stem, doubling every 15.7 stems.

The classical algorithm

  • Bidegree $(n, s)$ waits for $(n-1, s)$ and $(n+1, s-1)$.
  • In internal degree $t = n + s$, row-reduce the matrix of $d_s \colon F_s \to F_{s-1}$ over $\mathbb{F}_2$. Its image should be $\ker d_{s-1}$, known from $(n+1, s-1)$: add a generator of $F_s$ for each vector it misses.

Christian Nassau's algorithm

Use a finite subalgebra $B \subset A$

  • Take $B$ with profile $(p_1, p_2, \dots)$, such as $A(k)$. The signature of $\mathrm{Sq}(r_1, r_2, \dots)$ is $(r_1 \bmod 2^{p_1}, r_2 \bmod 2^{p_2}, \dots)$. There are $\dim B$ of them.
  • Zero step. Where $\operatorname{Ext}_B$ vanishes, one kernel over the signature-zero part, smaller by a factor of $\dim B$, finds the new generators.
  • Signature step. $\dim B - 1$ small corrections fix the differential.
220×
smaller matrices in the zero step than in the classical algorithm, by area, through stem 120
93%
of the time now goes to Milnor products, at stem 120

The $(n, s)$ plane, stems 0–400 · click a cell

Which subalgebra, where

$A(k)$ switches on along a line of slope $2^{k+1} - 2$ in $(n, s)$: $2, 6, 14, 30$ for $k = 1, \dots, 4$. Remember this picture.

Saving the resolution, with its quasi-inverses

Stem 400 would need over 12 petabytes of disk

Almost all of it is quasi-inverses: our copy of stem 256 held 39,000 bytes of them for every byte of differentials.

Two measurements: stem 200 (0.78 TB, an older format) and stem 256 (22.9 TB, from the README of the 2023 stem-256 dataset on Zenodo). The dashed curve's shape is computed, not fitted: the dense size of every classical matrix, from $\dim A_t$ and the generator counts. One constant matches stem 256; it then predicts 0.98 TB at stem 200.

Recompute, don't store

A quasi-inverse can be rebuilt from the tiny differentials, for about what it cost the first time.

Lift all the maps together, one bidegree at a time: each one is rebuilt once, and shared.

On disk: 23 TB → 0. And 3.8× faster than lifting map by map, on a 516-map test.

Two tracks at once

The usual suspects

  • Row reduction. The classical bottleneck. Nassau's algorithm shrinks the matrices, but they are still the biggest objects we build.
  • Milnor multiplication. The bottleneck since sseq adopted Nassau's algorithm in 2022: 93% of the time at stem 120.

In 2022 I asked Christian Nassau about GPUs, and guessed the gains were “potentially several orders of magnitude”. This year I worked on both at once.

Row reduction is mostly matrix multiplication

  • Row reduction is hard to parallelize. Each pivot waits for the one before, a poor fit for a GPU.
  • Blocked elimination. Reduce a narrow panel, then update the rest with one matrix product. The products are the $O(n^3)$ part.
  • Matrix multiplication is embarrassingly parallel. Every entry of $AB$ is independent.
-- forward pass over F₂, b columns at a time
for each panel of b columns, left to right:
  for each column j of the panel:   -- serial
    pick a row below the pivots with a 1 in j
    none? j is a free column: skip it
    swap it up; for each row r below it with a 1 in j:
      row r ← row r + pivot row;  L[r, j] ← 1
  -- k ≤ b pivots
        ┌ P  X ┐   P: the k pivot rows
        └ 0  Y ┘   Y: everything else

  Y ← Y + L · X                    -- one product
then back-substitute, right to left

Bunch and Hopcroft (1974); Ibarra, Moran and Hui (1982) for any rank: row reduction costs what matrix multiplication costs, up to a constant.

And NVIDIA had its own reason to build a 1-bit matrix multiplier.

Low-precision neural networks

Why NVIDIA built a 1-bit multiplier

Neural networks quantize their weights and inputs to make matrix products cheap, all the way down to one bit.

Quantizing to 0/1 is reducing mod 2: our use case exactly.

Where does each term $\mathrm{Sq}(T)$ go in the Milnor basis? · PR #270

Nassau's tables, in sseq at last

  • Nassau. Compute each term's position from a few small tables of dimensions of $\mathbb{F}_2[\xi_1, \dots, \xi_k]$.
  • sseq. A hash map: $O(1)$, and faster than the tables at small degrees.
  • The GPU port. The kernel needed a lookup it computes, not a hash map, so the port used Nassau's tables anyway. PR #270 brought them to the CPU.

At degree 400 the tables look up 2.7× faster, and the index on a stem-400 worker shrinks from 12.4 GB of hash maps to 2.1 GB of tables. Below degree ~300 the hash map wins: it falls out of cache only as the basis grows.

The reference for everything after it.

More hardware stopped helping

Bidegrees wait for each other: the dependencies form a directed acyclic graph, a DAG. However many workers we have, a run can't finish faster than its longest chain of dependencies. Measured on one GPU node, stems 0–250:

$T_P \;\ge\; \max\Big(\dfrac{W}{P},\; D\Big)$

time on $P$ workers, for total work $W$ and longest chain $D$. Past $P = W/D \approx 20$, more workers can't help much, whether we have 20 or 20,000.

Two reasons the chain is long: one bidegree per row at a time, and one signature at a time inside a bidegree.

A corner of the chart, schematic · click to replay

Shortening the chain between bidegrees

The picture behind the zero step · $B = A(1)$

$A$, seen from $B$

$A$ is free over $B$: copies of $B$, one for each element of $A/\!/B$. Signature zero gives a basis of $A/\!/B$.

Moving inside a copy is bookkeeping: the signature step. New generators come from jumping between copies, and the zero step sees only those jumps.

The first jump is $\mathrm{Sq}(4)$: in general $\mathrm{Sq}(2^{k+1})$ for $A(k)$.

PR #295

So a row only waits $\sigma$ back

Generators at $(n-j, s)$ reach $(n, s)$ only through $A/\!/A(k)$ in degree $j$, and that is zero for $0 < j < \sigma = 2^{k+1}$.

So computing $(n, s)$ needs only $(n - \sigma, s)$. Registering stays in order along the row, and it is cheap.

$\sigma = 2, 4, 8, 16, 32$ for $A(0)$ to $A(4)$. Same output.

Inside one bidegree

Why the signatures went one at a time

  • Order the signatures colexicographically, $\sigma_1 < \sigma_2 < \cdots < \sigma_N$. Step $i$ reads the $\sigma_i$-coordinates of one shared vector, the differential $dx$ being fixed, solves for a correction $c_i$, and writes it back: $dx \leftarrow dx + d(c_i)$.
  • $d(c_i)$ has coordinates only in signatures $\sigma_j \ge \sigma_i$. So step $j$ reads what steps $i < j$ wrote: a forward substitution, not $N$ independent solves.
  • Checked at stem 120: 33% of the entries a step reads had been changed by earlier steps (up to 44%), in 86% of bidegrees.

The signatures are a filtration, not a grading: corrections only go up. So which signatures feed which?

And it grows: $A(n)$ has $2^{(n+1)(n+2)/2}$ signatures, but its DAG is only $\binom{n+3}{3}$ deep. The width is exponential, the depth is a cubic: the further out we go, the more concurrency there is.

The stem-400 run, before running it

Pricing the work in advance

We can't measure a run we haven't done, so we price it: a cost model estimates each signature task's hours on an H200, from the sizes of its matrices. Beyond what we have computed, those sizes follow Burklund and Senger's growth law.

$\dfrac{W}{D} \approx 190$

On average, about 190 tasks could run at once, against 20 at stem 250 before the two DAGs. Workload scales ✓

From one machine to many

Other machines don't share our memory

Another node sees only what we send it.

So we need self-contained, well-defined tasks: pieces of work we can hand over whole.

We have them: the signature steps of Act III, each answered by a correction we add back.

Is the network fast enough? Who hands out the tasks? And in what order?

When is a task worth sending over the network?

$\dfrac{m}{\beta} \ll t$

$m$ bytes over a link of bandwidth $\beta$, against $t$, the time to compute the task.

Our H200 nodes' link is 25 Gb/s Ethernet: $\beta \approx 3$ GB/s.

$m$$m / \beta$$t$
A signature step, and its answer28 MB0.01 s1–2 min
A row reduction, to an H200 and back10–20 GB~5 s~4 min

Both comfortably. The row reductions are about 97% of the bytes. ✓

Who hands out the tasks

One coordinator, many workers, over TCP

  • The coordinator holds the resolution and the bidegree and signature DAGs, sends tasks, and merges the answers by XOR. It never computes.
  • A task is one signature step: a bidegree, a signature, and each generator's $d(x)$ there: a few hundred KB. Its correction comes back: a few tens of MB.
  • A worker keeps its own copy of the resolution: the coordinator sends every new generator to every worker.
  • An rref server is an H200 that only row-reduces. Workers send it their large matrices; cards without Hopper send all of them.

On the same four GPUs this is no faster. It is what lets any GPU on the cluster join.

In what order: dozens of GPUs, 190 tasks at a time

With dependencies, the order matters

Graham et al.'s notation: machines | constraints | objective

Scheduling a DAG on the fleet

  • The problem. $Q \mid \mathit{prec} \mid C_{\max}$: machines of different speeds, tasks in a DAG, finish as early as possible.
  • Plus memory. A card runs several tasks at once. Card $i$ has memory $M_i$, task $j$ needs $m_j$, and at every moment $\sum_{j \text{ on } i} m_j \le M_i$.
  • The easy case. Identical machines, no memory (Graham, 1966): any schedule that never idles finishes by $W/P + D$, at most twice the lower bound $\max(W/P, D)$.
  • Ours. Speeds differ by card and by kind of task ($R$, not $Q$), and every time is an estimate. A greedy scheduler can hand the critical task to the slowest card.

The scheduler's next version: the run itself used its predecessor

whelm: neither overwhelm nor underwhelm the machines

  • Prices every task's time and memory before it runs: sizes from the mathematics (extrapolated beyond what is computed), constants fitted to the census.
  • Learns each card's speed from the tasks it finishes.
  • Runs the longest remaining chain first, and packs each card up to its memory.
  • One message-driven core: every attempt idempotent, every decision in a replayable log.

Knowing when to stop

The costs kept moving under the scheduler, so we froze it: good enough beats optimal against a moving target.

Bob Bruner, a few years ago, paraphrased from memory

If you go by diagonals, you can tell the multinomial is zero as soon as you fill in a value, and the whole rest of the computation just disappears.
I remembered it on October 10, tracing $\mathrm{Sq}(4,2) \cdot \mathrm{Sq}(4,1)$ by hand.

$\mathrm{Sq}(4,2) \cdot \mathrm{Sq}(4,1)$, three ways

The matrix kernel

Build every matrix whose rows fit $R$, in odometer order. Check $S$ and the anti-diagonals once it is complete.

Two-sided

Fill from the bottom row up, within both budgets, skipping digits already used on each anti-diagonal.

Anti-diagonal

Fill the last anti-diagonal first; each finished one fixes two slacks, which are checked at once.

Two multiplication calls recorded from the live run on Oct 4, replayed on one H200

At scale

Changing what is enumerated beat tuning the kernel. Each took one or two days from idea to all 23 GPUs.

Why it suits the GPU

No dead ends, and nothing to store

Matrix kernelTwo-sidedAnti-diagonal
Matrices built that contribute, in degree 4360.006%27%all of them
Device memory68–91 GBunder 2 GBunder 2 GB
State per thread–360 bytes148 bytes
Busy threads per warp of 32–1220

A GPU runs 32 threads in lockstep: a thread that hits a dead end idles until its warp is done. Building only matrices that contribute keeps the warps busy on useful work, and needs no table of matrices in memory.

Cards without Hopper's instructions

  • Kernels are compiled at run time, for whatever card the worker lands on.
  • Only Hopper has the warpgroup 1-bit instruction our kernels use: the others send their large row reductions to an H200 over the network.
  • Under 2 GB of device memory is what lets a 16 GB V100 or a 24 GB A30 join at all.
  • Each new kind of card first redoes stems 0–200 and must match bit for bit: 0 mismatches.

PR #279 · Nassau's untwisted tensor resolutions

Every module, from the sphere's resolution?

  • Resolve $\mathbb{F}_2$ once. Tensor with $M$, and untwist with the antipode.
  • The differential is in closed form, so the tensor complex is never built. Works for infinite modules: the first example is $\mathbb{R}P^\infty$.
  • Stem 400 for every $M$, almost for free?
